summary: What prayer is; how to pray; the Lord’s Prayer as model; the relationship of prayer to God’s sovereignty
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 6:5-15, then Luke 11:1-13. Today is a doctrinal pause on prayer, so you are reading two accounts together. Notice that in Luke the disciples ask Jesus to teach them to pray, and he gives the prayer and then a parable and a promise.
settingTheScene: Yesterday you read the Lord’s Prayer within the Sermon on the Mount. Luke records a different occasion. Jesus had been praying, and when he finished, one of his disciples said, “Lord, teach us to pray.” Jesus gave them the pattern again in a slightly shorter form, and then taught about asking, seeking, and knocking. Together the two passages give a foundation for what the Bible teaches about prayer.
observation: “When you pray, you must not be like the hypocrites” (Matthew 6:5).
“Your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:8).
“Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).
“Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).
“Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples” (Luke 11:1).
“Father, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come” (Luke 11:2).
“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Luke 11:9).
“How much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13).
doctrinalFocus: Prayer is the means by which believers speak to God as their Father through Jesus Christ, in the power of the Holy Spirit. It includes praise, thanksgiving, confession, and petition. God does not need to be informed of what we need, and prayer does not change his purposes. Rather, he has chosen to bring about his purposes through the prayers of his people. We pray in Jesus’ name, which means that we come through his work and on his authority, not our own merit. Prayer is not a technique for getting what we want but a relationship in which we are conformed to the Father’s will.
interpretation:
Jesus’ teaching on prayer begins with how not to pray. Hypocrites pray to be seen, and pagans pile up words. Neither is how a child talks to a father. Jesus says to go into your room, close the door, and pray to your Father in secret. Real prayer is a personal conversation, not a performance.

The prayer itself begins with “Our Father.” This word alone changes everything. We are not approaching a distant ruler or a force. Through Christ we are children addressing a Father who loves us. Then come three petitions about God: his name be treated as holy, his kingdom come, his will be done. We start by wanting what he wants. Only then do we turn to ourselves: daily bread, forgiveness, and deliverance from the evil one. The order teaches us what to put first.

Luke adds a story. A man knocks at his friend’s door at midnight to borrow bread, and the friend gets up not out of friendship but because of the man’s persistence. Jesus’ point is a contrast: if even a reluctant neighbor responds, how much more will the Father? So we ask, seek, and knock. The verbs are in the present tense, suggesting continual asking.

And then the surprising conclusion. A father does not give a snake to a child who asks for a fish. If earthly parents, “who are evil,” give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him? The greatest answer to prayer is not an object but God himself, present in us by his Spirit. This does not mean that every request will be granted as we ask, but that the Father will always give what is good.
connection: Romans 8:15-16 says we have received the Spirit of adoption by whom we cry “Abba, Father.” Romans 8:26-27 says the Spirit helps us in our weakness when we do not know what to pray. John 14:13-14 teaches prayer in Jesus’ name. Hebrews 4:16 invites us to approach the throne of grace with confidence. 1 John 5:14 says that if we ask anything according to his will, he hears us. Philippians 4:6 says to make requests known to God with thanksgiving. James 4:2-3 warns about asking with wrong motives.
application:
Set aside a regular time and place to pray, even for ten minutes. Use the Lord’s Prayer as an outline: praise, God’s kingdom, daily needs, forgiveness, protection.

Keep a short list of requests you are bringing to the Father, and note when he answers.

Ask for the Holy Spirit, as Jesus invites, and ask specifically for help in a weakness.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that through Jesus you can call him Father.
Pray each petition of the Lord’s Prayer in your own words.
Ask him to teach you to pray with persistence.
